Here's a wild fact to kick us off:

The word "bank" — as in riverbank or as in Chase Bank — looks completely different to you depending on context. To a raw computer, it's just the same five letters. Getting machines to handle that ambiguity is one of the hardest problems in AI.

---

That's exactly what **tokenization** is trying to solve.

When you type a prompt, the LLM doesn't read words the way you do. It first chops your text into chunks called *tokens* — which might be whole words, parts of words, or even single characters.

[EX]The word "unbelievable" might become three tokens: "un" + "believ" + "able". GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens. The sentence "I went to the bank" becomes a sequence of number IDs — something like [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] — before the model ever "sees" it.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only form an LLM can actually process.[/KEY]

Those numbers are the raw input. Everything else the model does — understanding context, generating a reply — builds on top of that numerical sequence.

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A copy of a sentence stored in the model's memory
B) A chunk of text converted to a number — could be a word, part of a word, or a character
C) A single word, always
ANS: B
[/Q]

turns.user: I picked B) A chunk of text converted to a number — could be a word, part of a word, or a character
turns.reply:
That's exactly right — tokens are flexible chunks, not just whole words, and that flexibility is what lets the model handle any text thrown at it.

---

Now for the part that makes LLMs feel almost magical: **next-token prediction**.

After your prompt is tokenized into numbers, the model's entire job is deceptively simple — guess what token comes next, over and over, until the response is done.

It doesn't retrieve a stored answer. It doesn't search the web. It just keeps asking: *given everything so far, what token is most likely next?*

[EX]Finish this sentence: "The cat sat on the ___". The model assigns probabilities to every token in its 100K vocabulary. "mat" might get 34%, "floor" 18%, "couch" 12%, and so on. It picks from the high-probability options — and then repeats the whole process for the token after that.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates responses one token at a time, each chosen by probability — it is a next-token predictor, not a fact-retriever.[/KEY]

This is also why AI can sound fluent and confident while being completely wrong — it's optimizing for *plausible-sounding* next tokens, not for *true* ones.

[Q]
When an LLM generates a response, what is it actually doing?
A) Thinking through the problem the way a human would
B) Picking the most statistically likely next token, one at a time
C) Looking up the answer in a database it was trained on
ANS: B
[/Q]

turns.reply:
That's exactly right — tokens are chunks of text turned into numbers the model can actually work with.

Now here's where it gets interesting: what does the model *do* with those numbers?

---

After tokenization, the model runs those token IDs through something called the **attention mechanism**.

Attention lets the model look at every other token in your prompt when deciding what a given token means.

[EX]Remember "I went to the bank"? When the model processes "bank," attention lets it scan the whole sentence for clues. If nearby tokens include "river" or "fishing," it weights the nature meaning heavily. If it sees "deposit" or "loan," it weights the financial meaning. Same word, different context — attention sorts it out.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets the model weigh every word in context before deciding what any single word means — that's how ambiguity gets resolved.[/KEY]

This is why LLMs handle context so much better than older autocomplete tools, which only looked at the last word or two.

---

[Q]
Why does the attention mechanism matter for understanding language?
A) It lets the model consider the full context when interpreting each token
B) It checks the internet for the most likely meaning of ambiguous words
C) It memorizes which words appear together most often in training data
D) It looks up word definitions in a built-in dictionary
ANS: A
[/Q]

Picked up right where we left off — you've got tokenization and attention down.

Now for the final piece: what the model actually *outputs*.

---

After attention does its work, the model does something surprisingly simple: it **predicts the next token**.

It looks at all the tokens so far, runs them through its layers, and produces a probability distribution — a ranked list of what token is most likely to come next.

[EX]Give a model the prompt "The cat sat on the ___" and it assigns high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It picks from the high-probability options and outputs one token. Then it does the whole thing again for the token after that.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates text one token at a time, each token chosen based on probability — not lookup, not retrieval, not reasoning.[/KEY]

This is why AI can sound fluent and confident even when it's wrong — fluency comes from predicting likely-sounding tokens, not from checking facts.

That's the full pipeline: text → tokens → numbers → attention → next-token prediction → repeat.

---

[Q]
What is an LLM actually doing when it generates a response?
A) Searching the internet for the most relevant answer
B) Translating your question into a database query
C) Retrieving a stored answer from its training data
D) Predicting the most probable next token, one at a time
ANS: D
[/Q]

Here's a wild fact to kick us off:

The word "bank" in "I went to the bank to fish" and "I went to the bank to deposit money" looks identical to you — but an LLM has to figure out which meaning applies before it can say anything useful.

How does it even begin to do that? It starts by breaking your words into pieces.

---

When you type a prompt, the first thing an LLM does is **tokenization** — slicing your text into small chunks called *tokens*.

Tokens aren't always whole words. "Unhappiness" might become three tokens: "Un", "happi", "ness". Punctuation, spaces, even capitalization can split things differently.

[EX]GPT-4 uses a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. The sentence "Hello, world!" becomes about 4 tokens. A single emoji can be 3 tokens all by itself.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbered chunks — that's the only form an LLM can actually process.[/KEY]

Once you see text as a numbered list, you can start to ask: what number comes next?

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A single word, always — LLMs split text at spaces
B) A copy of a sentence the model memorized during training
C) A chunk of text (could be part of a word, a whole word, or punctuation) mapped to a number
ANS: C
[/Q]
